All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

Let $A:H\to K$ be a linear map ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces. Its singular values are the eigenvalues of
$|A|:=\sqrt{A^*A}:H\to H$, counted with multiplicity, as defined in
[[def-singular-values-of-an-endomorphism]]. Define the **trace norm**, or
Schatten-$1$ norm, by

$$\|A\|_1:=\sum_{j<\dim H}s_j(A).$$

The sum includes zero singular values and is $0$ when $H$ is the zero space.
For this definition, $A$ may be rectangular; the singular values are those of
$|A|$ on the domain $H$. The spectral trace formula is proved in
[[thm-qc-trace-norm-spectral-formula]].

For every linear map $A:H\to K$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces,

$$\|A\|_1=\operatorname{tr}_H\!\left(\sqrt{A^*A}\right).$$

Here $A^*A$ and its non-negative square root are endomorphisms of the domain
$H$; the trace is taken on $H$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

derivations.claim: Put $c:=\langle u|v\rangle_D$ and $s:=\sqrt{1-|c|^2}$. By [F3], $0\le s\le1$. If $s=0$, equality in Cauchy–Schwarz makes $v$ a unit scalar multiple of $u$, so $P_v=P_u$ and $D(P_u,P_v)=0$.

Suppose $s>0$ and set $e:=(v-cu)/s$. The Dirac convention makes $\langle u|e\rangle_D=0$, and direct expansion gives $\|e\|=1$. In the orthonormal basis $(u,e)$ of their span, $P_u-P_v$ has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}s^2&-cs\\-\overline c\,s&-s^2\end{pmatrix}$; it is zero on the orthogonal complement. This Hermitian matrix has trace $0$ and determinant $-s^2$, hence eigenvalues $s,-s$. By [F4]–[F6], $\|P_u-P_v\|_1=2s$, so $D(P_u,P_v)=s$.
For either case, $\|u-v\|^2=2-2\operatorname{Re}c\ge2(1-|c|)$, while $s^2=(1-|c|)(1+|c|)\le2(1-|c|)$. Thus $D(P_u,P_v)=s\le\|u-v\|$, including the $s=0$ case from step 1.1.

Let $A:H\to K$ be a linear map ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces. Its singular values are the eigenvalues of
$|A|:=\sqrt{A^*A}:H\to H$, counted with multiplicity, as defined in
[[def-singular-values-of-an-endomorphism]]. Define the **trace norm**, or
Schatten-$1$ norm, by

$$\|A\|_1:=\sum_{j<\dim H}s_j(A).$$

The sum includes zero singular values and is $0$ when $H$ is the zero space.
For this definition, $A$ may be rectangular; the singular values are those of
$|A|$ on the domain $H$. The spectral trace formula is proved in
[[thm-qc-trace-norm-spectral-formula]].

For every linear map $A:H\to K$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between finite-dimensional
complex inner-product spaces,

$$\|A\|_1=\operatorname{tr}_H\!\left(\sqrt{A^*A}\right).$$

Here $A^*A$ and its non-negative square root are endomorphisms of the domain
$H$; the trace is taken on $H$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

For a finite ordered family of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces
$H_k,K_k$ and complex-linear maps $T_k:H_k\to K_k$, the **tensor map**
$\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k:H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}\to
K_0\otimes\cdots\otimes K_{n-1}$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\left(\bigotimes_{k<n}T_k\right)(x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n-1})=T_0x_0\otimes\cdots\otimes T_{n-1}x_{n-1}.$$

For $n=0$, the tensor map is the identity map $z\mapsto z$ on the empty tensor
product $\mathbb C$.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.

derivations.claim: If either tensor factor is zero-dimensional, then $X=0$ and the claimed inequality follows from the empty coordinate sum in [F4]; assume both factors are nonzero for the rest of the proof. For any Hermitian $Z$ on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space, [F3] gives an orthonormal eigenbasis $(e_i)$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_i$. The adjoint identity [F11] and conjugate symmetry make $\lambda_i=\langle Ze_i,e_i\rangle=\langle e_i,Ze_i\rangle=\overline{\lambda_i}$, so each $\lambda_i$ is real. For every Hermitian $Y$ with $\|Y\|\le1$, [F12] gives $\operatorname{tr}(ZY)=\sum_i\lambda_i\langle Ye_i,e_i\rangle_{\rm root}$. Again [F11] makes each diagonal entry real, and [F8]–[F9] put it in $[-1,1]$. Thus $|\operatorname{tr}(ZY)|\le\sum_i|\lambda_i|=\|Z\|_1$: in the eigenbasis, $Z^\dagger Z$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_i^2$, so [F2] its nonnegative square root has eigenvalues $|\lambda_i|$, and [F1], [F2], [F12] give the trace norm sum. Equality is attained by the Hermitian contraction acting by $\operatorname{sgn}(\lambda_i)$ on each $e_i$ (and by $0$ when $\lambda_i=0$). Hence $\|Z\|_1=\sup_{Y=Y^\dagger,\ \|Y\|\le1}|\operatorname{tr}(ZY)|$.

Formula [F4] shows $\operatorname{Tr}_E X$ is Hermitian: transposing and conjugating its $(i,i')$ entry gives $\sum_j\overline{X_{(i',j),(i,j)}}=\sum_jX_{(i,j),(i',j)}$. If $Y=Y^\dagger$ and $\|Y\|\le1$, choose an orthonormal basis $(f_j)$ of $H_E$ by [F10] and write arbitrary $\xi=\sum_jx_j\otimes f_j$ and $\zeta=\sum_jy_j\otimes f_j$. The product inner product and tensor-map action [F6]–[F7] give $\langle(Y\otimes I_E)\xi,\zeta\rangle=\sum_j\langle Yx_j,y_j\rangle=\sum_j\langle x_j,Yy_j\rangle=\langle\xi,(Y\otimes I_E)\zeta\rangle$ by self-adjointness and [F11], so $Y\otimes I_E$ is Hermitian. Also [F6]–[F8] give $\|(Y\otimes I_E)\xi\|^2=\sum_j\|Yx_j\|^2\le\sum_j\|x_j\|^2=\|\xi\|^2$, so $\|Y\otimes I_E\|\le1$.

For the remaining nonzero-factor case, apply the variational identity in step 1.1 to $\operatorname{Tr}_E X$. For each allowed $Y$, [F5] and step 1.2 give $|\operatorname{tr}((\operatorname{Tr}_E X)Y)|=|\operatorname{tr}(X(Y\otimes I_E))|\le\|X\|_1$, using step 1.1 for the Hermitian contraction $Y\otimes I_E$. Taking the supremum proves the claimed inequality.

derivations.claim: From the product inner product [F2] and unit norm [F5], $\|Jx\|^2=\langle |0_A\rangle\otimes x,|0_A\rangle\otimes x\rangle=\|x\|^2$ for every $x$, so $J$ is an isometry by its definition in [F3]. Therefore $J^\dagger J=I_S$ by [F3]. It follows that $\Pi_0=JJ^\dagger$ is self-adjoint and idempotent, $\Pi_0\phi=Jq$, and $\phi=\Pi_0\phi+(I-\Pi_0)\phi$.

The two summands are orthogonal because $\Pi_0(I-\Pi_0)=0$ and $\Pi_0^\dagger=\Pi_0$. Expanding their squared norm by [F4] gives $1=\|\phi\|^2=\|\Pi_0\phi\|^2+\|(I-\Pi_0)\phi\|^2=\|q\|^2+p_\perp=p_0+p_\perp$. Both summands are nonnegative, so each lies in $[0,1]$.

If $p_0>0$, then $\|q/\sqrt{p_0}\|^2=p_0/p_0=1$. If $p_0=0$, definiteness of the inner-product norm gives $q=0$, so normalization is undefined and the definition correctly assigns no conditional vector.

**Input:** An LCU representation and complete PREPARE and SELECT access from [[def-qa-21-lcu-input-and-access-model]], including their stated work-register and padded-index behavior. The access record must explicitly supply PREPARE$^\dagger$ and its cost; an input without that inverse access is inadmissible.

**Procedure:** On the coefficient/work ancillas and system, apply PREPARE, then SELECT, then the supplied PREPARE$^\dagger$. Return the complete unitary $W=P^\dagger S_{\rm sel}P$. Charge the three calls at their declared costs. No measurement or deterministic state-output guarantee is part of this procedure.

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). For vectors $x,y$ in the same
space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and
$x\in K$, define the rank-one linear map

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

For an integer $d\ge 1$, the $d$-level register is the complex inner-product
space $Q_d=\mathbb C^d$ with the standard pairing
$\langle z,w\rangle_{\rm root}=\sum_{j<d}z_j\overline{w_j}$, linear in the
first argument as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]] and
[[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]. Its **computational basis** is the
ordered standard basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]].
The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over
$\mathbb C$ of $n$ copies of $Q_2$. Here $\otimes_{\mathbb C}$ is the algebraic
module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor
product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. This one-dimensional trivial
register is distinct from the zero vector space $\mathbb C^0$. By definition a
register has positive dimension; a zero-dimensional space may still occur as a
factor in the more general tensor-space construction below.

Let $A$ be a finite register with distinguished unit computational-basis vector $|0_A\rangle$ (unit by [[thm-qc-computational-basis-orthonormal]]), let $S$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space, and define the isometry $J:S\to A\otimes S$ by $Jx=|0_A\rangle\otimes x$. The product inner product makes $J$ an isometry; [[lem-qc-linear-isometry-adjoint-identities]] gives $J^\dagger J=I_S$, and [[thm-qc-isometric-encoding-projector]] makes $\Pi_0:=JJ^\dagger$ the orthogonal projection onto its image. On elementary tensors this is $|0_A\rangle\langle0_A|\otimes I_S$ by the convention of [[def-qc-tensor-map]]. For a unit vector $\phi\in A\otimes S$, define its zero-branch vector $q:=J^\dagger\phi$, zero-branch weight $p_0:=\|q\|^2$, and complementary-branch weight $p_\perp:=\|(I-\Pi_0)\phi\|^2$. When $p_0>0$, the conditional system vector is $q/\sqrt{p_0}$; when $p_0=0$, no conditional vector is assigned. This definition fixes only the clean-ancilla two-outcome branch rule used on this page; it makes no physical realization claim.

With the notation of [[def-qa-21-clean-ancilla-postselection]], every unit vector $\phi$ has $p_0,p_\perp\in[0,1]$ and $p_0+p_\perp=1$. If $p_0>0$, the assigned conditional vector $q/\sqrt{p_0}$ is a unit vector; if $p_0=0$, then $q=0$ and no conditional vector exists.

For every $d\ge1$, the ordered computational basis $(e_0,\ldots,e_{d-1})$ of
the register $Q_d$ from [[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]] is an
orthonormal basis for its declared inner product. Separately, the one-dimensional
zero-qubit register has the basis $\{1\}$ by definition.

derivations.claim: Write $\beta_j=\sqrt{|c_j|/\alpha}$ and $\omega_j=c_j/|c_j|$ for $c_j\ne0$ (take $\omega_j=1$ when $c_j=0$). PREPARE gives $e^{i\theta}\sum_{j<m}\beta_j|j,0_{\rm work}\rangle$ from the all-zero ancilla. After SELECT, the $j$th component is $e^{i\theta}\beta_j|j,0_{\rm work}\rangle\otimes\omega_jV_j\psi$. Apply [F3] to $\phi=WJ\psi$: its zero-branch vector is $J^\dagger WJ\psi=M\psi/\alpha$. Its branch weight is therefore $\|M\psi\|^2/\alpha^2$, and [F4] makes this a valid probability in $[0,1]$.
If $\|M\psi\|>0$, division of the branch vector by its norm gives $M\psi/\|M\psi\|$. If $M\psi=0$, the weight is zero and [F4] forbids assigning a normalized conditional vector to that branch.

Let $H=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}a_jV_j$ on a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space, with $m\ge1$, real $a_j$ and Hermitian unitaries $V_j$, and put $\Lambda=\sum_j|a_j|$. For real $h$ and integer $K\ge0$, define
$$M_K(h):=\sum_{k=0}^{K}\frac{(-ihH)^k}{k!}.$$
Its ordered product-term LCU list has one empty tuple for $k=0$, with coefficient $1$ and unitary $I$, and for each $1\le k\le K$ and ordered tuple $(j_1,\ldots,j_k)$ has coefficient
$$c_{k,\mathbf j}:=\frac{(-i)^k h^k a_{j_1}\cdots a_{j_k}}{k!}$$
and unitary $V_{j_1}\cdots V_{j_k}$. Distinct tuples remain distinct entries even if their product unitaries coincide. The absolute coefficient sum of this listed representation is
$$s_K(h):=\sum_{k=0}^{K}\frac{(\Lambda|h|)^k}{k!}.$$

Whenever $s_K(h)\le2$, append two distinct identity entries with coefficients $+q$ and $-q$, where $q=(2-s_K(h))/2$. They leave the represented matrix unchanged and raise the listed absolute coefficient sum to exactly $2$. If $q=0$, the zero-weight entries may be retained with zero preparation amplitude or omitted. The polynomial, coefficient phases, ordered tuple index, and any numerical precision used to generate them are part of the finite input/access record; no term product, coefficient table, PREPARE circuit, or SELECT circuit is free.

In this page a **Hamiltonian** is a self-adjoint endomorphism $H$ of a
finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $V$; no physical postulate is
part of the term. Let $\sigma(H)$ be the set of its distinct eigenvalues and
let $P_\lambda$ be the orthogonal projection onto the $\lambda$-eigenspace.
For real time $t$, define the finite matrix evolution

$$U_H(t):=\sum_{\lambda\in\sigma(H)}e^{-it\lambda}P_\lambda = f_t(H),\qquad f_t(\lambda)=e^{-it\lambda}.$$

The second expression uses the finite spectral functional calculus
[[def-functional-calculus-for-a-normal-endomorphism]]. If $V$ is the zero
space, the spectrum is empty and the empty sum is the unique endomorphism,
which is also the identity on $V$. This definition specifies a mathematical
unitary from a finite matrix; it makes no claim that the operation has an
efficient circuit or a free access cost.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].
For every $z\in\mathbb C$, the series $\sum z^n/n!$ converges absolutely.

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], choose an orthonormal eigenbasis of $H$ with eigenvalues $\lambda$. For a unit eigenvector $u_\lambda$, $|\lambda|=\|Hu_\lambda\|=\|\sum_j a_jV_ju_\lambda\|\le\sum_j|a_j|\|V_ju_\lambda\|=\Lambda$ by [F2]–[F4]. On this basis, [L1] and [L2] make the difference diagonal with scalar entries $\sum_{k=0}^K(-ih\lambda)^k/k!-\exp(-ih\lambda)$.
Since $x\ge0$, the finite Taylor coefficient sum obeys $0\le s_K=\sum_{k=0}^Kx^k/k!\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}x^k/k!=e^x$ by [L1] and [F5]. If $x\le\ln2$, [F7] gives $s_K\le e^x\le2$.

Put $n=K+1$. The absolute scalar-series tail at eigenvalue $\lambda$ is at most $\sum_{k=n}^{\infty}(|h||\lambda|)^k/k!$. Writing $k=n+j$ and using $(n+j)!\ge n!j!$ bounds this by $(|h||\lambda|)^n/n!\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}(|h||\lambda|)^j/j!=e^{|h||\lambda|}(|h||\lambda|)^n/n!$ by [F5]–[F6]. If the diagonal error has entries $d_i$ in the eigenbasis and $z=\sum_i z_i u_i$, then its squared output norm is $\sum_i|d_i|^2|z_i|^2\le(\max_i|d_i|)^2\|z\|^2$; an eigenbasis vector attaining the finite maximum gives equality in the operator norm [F4]. Hence the operator norm is $\max_i|d_i|$. Since $0\le|h||\lambda_i|\le x$, the monotonicity of $e^u$ and $u^n$ on nonnegative reals gives $e^{|h||\lambda_i|}|h|^n|\lambda_i|^n/n!\le e^xx^n/n!$. Taking the maximum proves the stated tail bound.

Assume $x\le\ln2$, so $e^x\le2$ by [F7]. Let $L=\ln(1/\eta)$. The exponential series gives $2<e<3$: its first two terms sum to $2$, while $1/k!\le2^{-(k-1)}$ for $k\ge2$, with strict inequality for $k\ge3$, so the remaining sum is less than $1$. Thus $\exp(0)=1<2<\exp(1)=e$ by [F5], and the strict increase and inverse relation in [F7] give $0<\ln2<1$. If $L<1$, $n=10$ gives $2x^{10}/10!<2/10!<1/3<e^{-1}<\eta$. If $L\ge1$, take $n=\lceil16eL/\ln(e+L)\rceil$. For $z\ge1$, $g(z)=\sqrt z-\ln z$ has derivative $g'(z)=(\sqrt z-2)/(2z)$, so it decreases up to $z=4$ and increases thereafter. Since $e>2$, $\exp(2)=e^2>4$, hence $\ln4<2$ by [F7]; thus $g(z)\ge g(4)=2-\ln4>0$. Also $e+L<4L$. Therefore $$\frac ne\ge\frac{16L}{\ln(e+L)}\ge\frac{16L}{\sqrt{e+L}}>4\sqrt{e+L},$$ so $\ln(n/e)>\tfrac12\ln(e+L)$. Hence $n\ln(n/e)\ge8eL\ge L+\ln4$, using $e>2$, $L\ge1$, and $\ln4<2$. For the factorial estimate, monotonicity of $\ln s$ gives $\ln(n!)=\sum_{k=1}^n\ln k\ge\int_1^n\ln s\,ds=n\ln n-n+1$, so $n!\ge(n/e)^n\ge e^{L+\ln4}=4/\eta$. Since $e^xx^n/n!\le2/n!$, this choice gives a tail at most $\eta/2\le\eta$. In both cases $n=O(1+L/\ln(e+L))$. Since $\ln(e+e^L)\le L+\ln2\le e+L$, this is also $O(1+L/\ln\ln(e+e^L))$, the displayed order after changing logarithm bases. Hence $K=n-1$ has the stated order.

**Input:** A unitary $W$ on coefficient/work ancillas and system, explicit inverse access to $W$, the reflection $R_0=I-2\Pi_0$ of [[def-qa-21-oblivious-reflection]], and an operator $M$ satisfying $J^\dagger WJ=M/2$ for the clean injection $Jx=|0_{\rm anc}\rangle\otimes x$.

**Procedure:** Chronologically apply $W$, then $R_0$, then $W^\dagger$, then $R_0$, then $W$. The resulting unitary is
$$C:=-WR_0W^\dagger R_0W.$$
The scalar $-1$ is an explicit phase correction; it is not omitted when this procedure is controlled. The circuit uses two $W$ calls, one $W^\dagger$ call, and two reflection calls. A controlled invocation requires the declared controlled forward, inverse, reflection, and phase-correction gates. This procedure makes no measurement and asserts no exact ancilla cleanup for a nonunitary or approximate $M$; the robust clean-input guarantee is proved separately.

Let $A$ be the full coefficient and PREPARE-work ancilla register in [[def-qa-21-lcu-input-and-access-model]], let $S$ be the system, and let $J:S\to A\otimes S$ be the clean injection of [[def-qa-21-clean-ancilla-postselection]]. Set $\Pi_0:=JJ^\dagger$; [[thm-qc-isometric-encoding-projector]] makes this the orthogonal projection onto the image of $J$. Its basis formula is $\Pi_0=|0_A\rangle\langle0_A|\otimes I_S$, where $|0_A\rangle$ is unit by [[thm-qc-computational-basis-orthonormal]] and the tensor action is that of [[def-qc-tensor-map]]. Define
$$R_0:=I-2\Pi_0.$$
Thus $R_0$ acts as $-I$ on the clean-ancilla subspace and as $+I$ on its orthogonal complement; it acts identically on the unknown system state. In the convention of [[def-qc-reflection]], $R_0=S_{\Pi_0}$, while that item writes $R_{\Pi_0}=2\Pi_0-I=-R_0$. These signs are distinct inside controlled blocks: if only the controlled $R_{\Pi_0}$ is supplied, implement controlled $R_0$ with the exact control-$Z$ correction of [[thm-qc-reflection-unitary-involution]] and charge that gate. A projector-reflection call and its controlled form are explicit access operations, not free consequences of a state vector.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and let $\Pi$ be an orthogonal projection. The operators $R_\Pi=2\Pi-I$ and $S_\Pi=I-2\Pi$ are self-adjoint unitary involutions, with $R_\Pi=-S_\Pi$. On $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$ they act as $+I$ and $-I$, respectively; on $\ker\Pi$ they act as $-I$ and $+I$. In control-first order,

$$C(S_\Pi)=(Z_C)C(R_\Pi),\qquad Z_C:=\operatorname{diag}(I_H,-I_H)=Z\otimes I_H.$$

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

Let $H,K$ be finite-dimensional (have finite bases by [[def-dimension]])
complex inner-product spaces and let
$V:H\to K$ be a linear isometry. Then $V^\dagger V=I_H$. If $V$ is also
surjective, then $VV^\dagger=I_K$.

Let $\mathcal H_L,\mathcal H_P$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let $V:\mathcal H_L\to\mathcal H_P$ be a linear isometry. Then $V^*V=I_{\mathcal H_L}$. derivations.claim: By [F10], $J^\dagger J=I$ and $\Pi$ is an orthogonal projection. By the circuit order in [L1], the factors in $C$ are unitary by [F2]–[F4], so $CJ$ is an isometry. Put $D:=J^\dagger CJ$. By [F1] and the minus sign in $C$, $D=3M/2-MM^\dagger M/2$. Write $E=M-V$. For every unit vector $x$, $\|Mx\|\le\|Vx\|+\|Ex\|\le1+\eta$, so $\|M\|\le1+\eta$ by [F5]. For each endomorphism $T$ of the nonzero space $S$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\|Tx\|=\max_{\|y\|=1}|\langle Tx,y\rangle|$ (with $Tx=0$ immediate), hence $\|T\|=\max_{\|x\|=\|y\|=1}|\langle Tx,y\rangle|$. The adjoint identity interchanges the unit vectors, so $\|T^\dagger\|=\|T\|$; in particular $\|M^\dagger\|\le1+\eta$ and $\|E^\dagger\|=\|E\|\le\eta$.

Since $VV^\dagger V=V$, $MM^\dagger M-V=(M-V)M^\dagger M+V(M^\dagger-V^\dagger)M+VV^\dagger(M-V)$. For every unit vector, apply the vector triangle inequality [F6] and [F7] to these three terms; using $\|E^\dagger\|=\|E\|\le\eta$ and $\|V\|=\|V^\dagger\|=1$ from [F4] gives $\|MM^\dagger M-V\|\le\eta((1+\eta)^2+(1+\eta)+1)$. Maximizing over unit vectors by [F5], $\|D-V\|\le\frac32\eta+\frac12\eta((1+\eta)^2+(1+\eta)+1)\le4\eta$ for $\eta\le1/100$.

Let $L=(I-\Pi)CJ$. Since $\Pi=JJ^\dagger$ and $J^\dagger J=I$ by [F10], $CJ=JD+L$ and $J^\dagger L=J^\dagger(I-JJ^\dagger)CJ=J^\dagger CJ-(J^\dagger J)J^\dagger CJ=0$. Hence both cross terms vanish in $(CJ)^\dagger CJ=(JD+L)^\dagger(JD+L)$, and $D^\dagger D+L^\dagger L=(CJ)^\dagger CJ=I$ because $C$ and $J$ are isometries. Thus $L^\dagger L=I-D^\dagger D$ and $\|L\|^2=\|I-D^\dagger D\|$ by [F7].

Set $\delta=\|D-V\|\le4\eta$ by step 2.1. For every unit vector $x$, $\|Dx\|\le\|Vx\|+\|(D-V)x\|\le1+\delta$, so $\|D\|\le1+\delta$. Since $V^\dagger V=I$, $I-D^\dagger D=(V-D)^\dagger D+V^\dagger(V-D)$; the vector triangle inequality [F6] and [F7] therefore give $\|(I-D^\dagger D)x\|\le\delta\|D\|+\delta\le\delta(2+\delta)$ for unit $x$. Maximizing by [F5], $\|I-D^\dagger D\|\le\delta(2+\delta)\le4\eta(2+4\eta)\le9\eta$. Thus $\|L\|\le3\sqrt{\eta}$.

From $CJ-JV=J(D-V)+L$, for every unit $x$ the vector triangle inequality [F6] and the isometry of $J$ in [F10] give $\|(CJ-JV)x\|\le\|D-V\|+\|L\|\le4\eta+3\sqrt\eta$. Maximizing by [F5] and using $\eta\le1/100$ yields $\|CJ-JV\|\le10\sqrt\eta$.

For any finite reference space $R$, choose an orthonormal basis $(e_j)$ by [F9] and write $\xi=\sum_jx_j\otimes e_j$. By [F8], $\|(CJ-JV)\otimes I_R\,\xi\|^2=\sum_j\|(CJ-JV)x_j\|^2\le(10\sqrt\eta)^2\sum_j\|x_j\|^2=(10\sqrt\eta)^2\|\xi\|^2$. Thus the same clean-input isometry bound holds with any finite reference, including entangled inputs.

The description of $\epsilon$ supplies arbitrarily tight rational interval enclosures. Also supply the complete PREPARE/SELECT, inverse, and cost interfaces from [[def-qa-21-lcu-input-and-access-model]] for the Taylor list selected below. For the certified procedure the real descriptions supply arbitrarily tight rational interval enclosures for $S=\Lambda|t|$ and $S/\ln2$, where $\Lambda=\sum_j|a_j|$. Exact coefficient phases and the required unitary/circuit access for the selected list are separate supplied data; interval names alone do not provide them. Arithmetic, refinement, description and generation costs are charged separately. No efficient classical compiler is asserted.

For the **indexed term-query implementation**, additionally supply the complete unitary $T(|j\rangle\otimes x)=|j\rangle\otimes V_jx$ for $j<m$, acting as identity at padded term indices, together with every controlled or inverse form actually used and its separate costs. A call to this coherent multiplexer is one indexed term query. Individual accesses to the separate $V_j$ do not grant this operation: when it is assembled from individual controlled $V_j$, each multiplexed call uses $m$ equality-controlled individual calls, and all label tests, routing, phase gates and work are charged. With an independently supplied Taylor SELECT, only its declared internal resource record applies.

**Procedure:**

1. Refine an enclosure $[\epsilon_-,\epsilon_+]$ of $\epsilon$ until $0<\epsilon_-$ and $\epsilon_+\le2\epsilon_-$. Refine an enclosure $[S_-,S_+]$ of $S=\Lambda|t|$, intersecting with the known nonnegative half-line, until its width is less than $\epsilon_-/8$. If $S_+\le\epsilon_-/4$, return the exact identity circuit with no oracle calls and the certificate $S\le\epsilon/4$. Otherwise proceed to the segmented branch; no positive lower bound on $S$ is needed. These refinements terminate because $\epsilon>0$ and the supplied descriptions give arbitrarily tight rational enclosures. No exact equality test on interval-described reals is used; every $t=0$ or $\Lambda=0$ input takes the identity branch.
2. In the remaining branch put $q=S/\ln2$. In the ideal exact-arithmetic variant set $r=\max(1,\lceil q\rceil)$. In the certified variant refine an enclosure $[q_-,q_+]$ until its width is less than $1$, then set $r=\max(1,\lceil q_+\rceil)$. Either choice has $r\ge1$, $\Lambda|t|/r\le\ln2$, and $r<q+2$. Set $h=t/r$ and $\eta=\epsilon^2/(1600r^2)$. All refinement and segment-count costs are recorded.
3. Set $\eta_-:=\epsilon_-^2/(1600r^2)$, a positive rational lower bound for $\eta$. Set $n=1$ and successively double $n$ until the exact rational comparison $4/n!\le\eta_-$ holds; compute the factorial by finite integer multiplication and set $K=n-1$. This finite scheduler has no real-equality test or unbounded refinement at a fixed failed order. Since $x=\Lambda|h|\le\ln2<1$, the tail in [[thm-qa-21-taylor-tail-bound]] is at most $2/n!\le\eta_-/2\le\eta/2$. Its factorial estimate gives the stated logarithmic-over-double-logarithmic order, including the factor of at most two from doubling. Charge the factorial and coefficient arithmetic.
4. Expand $M_K(h)$ into the ordered product-term LCU list of [[def-qa-21-truncated-taylor-lcu]]. The certificate $\Lambda|h|\le\ln2$ and [[thm-qa-21-taylor-tail-bound]] prove $s_K\le2$ analytically. Add two distinct identity terms $+qI,-qI$ with $q=(2-s_K)/2$, retaining zero-weight padding labels if needed; the matrix is unchanged and the listed norm is exactly $2$. Under the indexed term-query implementation, implement each Taylor SELECT using at most $K$ controlled indexed term queries: process tuple positions from $K$ down to $1$, condition each call on a valid tuple having that position, and use its term label. Compute/uncompute those labels in charged work registers. This reverse execution order yields the displayed product $V_{j_1}\cdots V_{j_k}$. Apply the coefficient phase separately and act as identity on padding and unused labels. The adjoint SELECT reverses this sequence and uses the declared inverse calls.
5. For each of the $r$ segments, allocate a fresh clean register containing the expanded-term index and every PREPARE work wire. Build $W=P^\dagger S_{\rm sel}P$ using the exact coefficient phases and the padded invalid-index behavior. Apply the phase-corrected chronological circuit $W,R_0,W^\dagger,R_0,W$, with $R_0=I-2\Pi_0$ on the complete clean coefficient/work register. Thus the segment unitary is $-WR_0W^\dagger R_0W$, with two reflection calls, two forward $W$ calls, and one inverse call.
6. Compose the $r$ segment circuits in time order. Retain every segment's coefficient/work register in the output dilation; do not measure or claim exact cleanup. $$M_K(h):=\sum_{k=0}^{K}\frac{(-ihH)^k}{k!}.$$
Its ordered product-term LCU list has one empty tuple for $k=0$, with coefficient $1$ and unitary $I$, and for each $1\le k\le K$ and ordered tuple $(j_1,\ldots,j_k)$ has coefficient
$$c_{k,\mathbf j}:=\frac{(-i)^k h^k a_{j_1}\cdots a_{j_k}}{k!}$$
and unitary $V_{j_1}\cdots V_{j_k}$. Distinct tuples remain distinct entries even if their product unitaries coincide. The absolute coefficient sum of this listed representation is
$$s_K(h):=\sum_{k=0}^{K}\frac{(\Lambda|h|)^k}{k!}.$$

Whenever $s_K(h)\le2$, append two distinct identity entries with coefficients $+q$ and $-q$, where $q=(2-s_K(h))/2$. $$\left\|M_K(h)-e^{-ihH}\right\|\le e^x\frac{x^{K+1}}{(K+1)!}.$$
The Taylor coefficient sum $s_K=\sum_{k=0}^Kx^k/k!$ satisfies $s_K\le e^x\le2$ when $x\le\ln2$. If $0<\eta<1$ and $x\le\ln2$, there is a $K=O\!\left(1+\frac{\log(1/\eta)}{\log\log(e+1/\eta)}\right)$ for which the right-hand side is at most $\eta$.

In this page a **Hamiltonian** is a self-adjoint endomorphism $H$ of a
finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $V$; no physical postulate is
part of the term. Let $\sigma(H)$ be the set of its distinct eigenvalues and
let $P_\lambda$ be the orthogonal projection onto the $\lambda$-eigenspace.
For real time $t$, define the finite matrix evolution

$$U_H(t):=\sum_{\lambda\in\sigma(H)}e^{-it\lambda}P_\lambda = f_t(H),\qquad f_t(\lambda)=e^{-it\lambda}.$$

The second expression uses the finite spectral functional calculus
[[def-functional-calculus-for-a-normal-endomorphism]]. If $V$ is the zero
space, the spectrum is empty and the empty sum is the unique endomorphism,
which is also the identity on $V$. This definition specifies a mathematical
unitary from a finite matrix; it makes no claim that the operation has an
efficient circuit or a free access cost.

Let $H$ be a self-adjoint endomorphism of a finite-dimensional complex
inner-product space $V$. For real $t,s$, the evolution from
[[def-qa-19-finite-matrix-dynamics]] satisfies
$$U_H(0)=I_V,\qquad U_H(t)^*U_H(t)=I_V,\qquad U_H(t+s)=U_H(t)U_H(s),\qquad \frac{d}{dt}U_H(t)=-iHU_H(t).$$
Moreover, $U_H$ is the unique differentiable map $Y:\mathbb R\to
\operatorname{End}(V)$ satisfying $Y'(t)=-iHY(t)$ and $Y(0)=I_V$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $H=H^*$ be a specified endomorphism. Its exact time-$t$ evolution is $U_H(t)=e^{-itH}$ as defined by [[def-qa-19-finite-matrix-dynamics]]. The notation $\|T\|$ denotes the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]. The target register's Hilbert space is identified with $V$ as part of the input. A **Hamiltonian simulator at encoded time $t$ and tolerance $0<\epsilon<1$** is a declared procedure whose output is a unitary $W$ on the stated target register satisfying $\|W-U_H(t)\|\le\epsilon$. If its circuit uses auxiliary registers, the exact clean or dirty contract of [[def-qc-clean-and-dirty-ancillas]] must make the induced target unitary $W$ well-defined; the error is measured on that target unitary. The scalar time and tolerance have exact finite descriptions under the declared input convention; their description lengths are recorded.

The resource record lists, separately, the number of calls to each named oracle, controlled calls, inverse calls, elementary gate occurrences, clean and dirty ancillary wires, coefficient bits, full circuit-description bits, and classical generation time. A coordinate not supplied by the access contract is unavailable, not zero. No matrix description supplies a circuit, oracle, controlled call, inverse call, or term exponential for free; uniform-family and cost conventions are those of [[def-qc-uniform-circuit-family]], [[def-qc-circuit-cost-model]], [[def-qc-controlled-unitary-access]], and [[def-qc-inverse-unitary-access]]. No polynomial resource bound is asserted by this definition.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with the root library's convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$; non-negative and trace have the meanings of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]] and [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. The zero-dimensional space is excluded: its only endomorphism has trace $0$.

Here $\ker\rho=\{x\in H:\rho x=0\}$, using the kernel of a linear map from [[def-kernel-and-image-of-a-linear-map]]. The **support** of $\rho$ is the orthogonal complement of its kernel in the root convention:

$$\operatorname{supp}(\rho):=\{x\in H: \langle x,y\rangle=0\text{ for every }y\in\ker\rho\}.$$

For a subspace $S\subseteq H$, $\rho$ is **faithful on $S$** when $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)=S$ and the restriction $\rho|_S:S\to S$ is positive definite in the sense of [[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]. This restriction is an endomorphism: if $x\in S$ and $y\in\ker\rho$, self-adjointness gives $\langle\rho x,y\rangle=\langle x,\rho y\rangle=0$, so $\rho x\in(\ker\rho)^\perp=S$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let $u,v\in H$ be unit vectors. Write $P_u=|u\rangle\langle u|$ and $P_v=|v\rangle\langle v|$ using the Dirac convention of [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]], and define their trace distance by $D(P_u,P_v):=\tfrac12\|P_u-P_v\|_1$, where $\|\cdot\|_1$ is the trace norm of [[def-qc-trace-norm]]. Then
$$D(P_u,P_v)\le \|u-v\|.$$

Let $H_A,H_E$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces and let $X=X^\dagger$ be an endomorphism of $H_A\otimes H_E$. Then
$$\|\operatorname{Tr}_E X\|_1\le\|X\|_1.$$
The trace norm and partial trace are those of [[def-qc-trace-norm]] and [[def-qc-partial-trace]]. If either factor is zero-dimensional, both sides are zero.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be
linear. Choose any ordered basis $\mathcal B$ of $V$ and define the **trace of
the endomorphism $T$** by

$$\operatorname{tr}(T):=\operatorname{tr}([T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal B}).$$

This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in
two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace. When
$V$ is the zero space, the empty basis gives trace $0$.
Every finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space has an orthonormal basis. In dimension zero, this is the empty basis.

derivations.claim: On the identity branch let $S=\Lambda|t|\le\epsilon/4\le1/4<1$. In an orthonormal eigenbasis as in [F2], each Hamiltonian eigenvalue satisfies $|\lambda|\le\Lambda$. Its scalar-series error obeys $|e^{-it\lambda}-1|\le\sum_{k\ge1}S^k/k!\le\sum_{k\ge1}S^k=S/(1-S)\le\epsilon/(4-\epsilon)\le\epsilon/3$. The diagonal norm calculation in [F2] proves $\|I-U_H(t)\|\le\epsilon/3$, and the error is zero if $t=0$ or $\Lambda=0$. Otherwise step 2 chooses a finite $r$ with $x:=\Lambda|t|/r\le\ln2$; no lower bound on $S$ is needed. Hence $s_K\le e^x\le2$, and cancelling padding makes the norm exactly $2$ without changing $M_K$.

By [F3], the padded circuit has block $M_K(h)/2$. The uncorrected amplified block is $-3M_K(h)/2+M_K(h)M_K(h)^\dagger M_K(h)/2$ by [F4], so the explicit phase correction in [L1] gives the corresponding opposite-sign block; [F5] supplies the needed full isometry estimate including leakage. The Taylor-tail rule gives $\|M_K(h)-U_H(h)\|\le\eta$, and $\eta\le1/1600<1/100$. Apply [F5] with $V=U_H(h)$ to obtain a clean-input isometry error at most $10\sqrt\eta=\epsilon/(4r)$ for each segment, including any finite reference and all earlier retained registers.

By [L1], the scheduler uses the positive rational $\eta_-:=\epsilon_-^2/(1600r^2)$, where $\eta/4\le\eta_-\le\eta$. The loop terminates because $n!$ tends to infinity. Since $\epsilon_-\le\epsilon\le1$ and $r\ge1$, $\eta_-\le1/1600$; hence $L_-:=\ln(4/\eta_-)>1$. For $N=\lceil16eL_-/\ln(e+L_-)\rceil$, the inequalities $\ln(e+L_-)\le\sqrt{e+L_-}$ and $e+L_-<4L_-$ give $N/e>4\sqrt{e+L_-}$, hence $\ln(N/e)>\tfrac12\ln(e+L_-)$. Therefore $N\ln(N/e)\ge8eL_-\ge L_-+\ln4$. Monotonicity of $\ln s$ gives $\ln(N!)=\sum_{k=1}^N\ln k\ge\int_1^N\ln s\,ds=N\ln N-N+1$, so $N!\ge(N/e)^N\ge4/\eta_-$. The least power of two at least $N$ is less than $2N$ and already meets the factorial comparison, so the scheduler stops at some $n<2N$. Thus $K=n-1=O(1+L_-/\ln(e+L_-))$. Since $\eta/4\le\eta_-\le\eta$ and $\eta\le1/1600$, this is $O(1+\log(1/\eta)/\log\log(e+1/\eta))$. The rule uses only a finite integer loop, and its cost is a separate classical coordinate. For the error estimates, $e^xx^n/n!\le2/n!\le\eta_-/2\le\eta/2$ because $x\le\ln2<1$.

The ideal segment maps each input to the same system evolution $U_H(h)$ and a fresh zero register. Telescoping the $r$ compositions, every intervening exact segment is an isometry and has norm $1$, so the total access-circuit isometry error is at most $r\epsilon/(4r)=\epsilon/4$. The ideal system factor is $U_H(h)^r=U_H(t)$ by [F6].

Replacing the exact access calls by their compiled unitaries changes the full circuit in operator norm by at most the sum of their per-call errors: expand the product difference as a telescoping sum and use norm $1$ for each unitary factor. The declared sum is at most $\epsilon/2$ by [L1]. The triangle inequality therefore gives $\|V_{\rm impl}J_{\rm in}-J_{\rm out}U_H(t)\|\le\epsilon/4+\epsilon/2=3\epsilon/4\le\epsilon$.

First take a pure unit input, including any finite reference. The segmented isometry bound in step 3.1, or the identity-branch bound in step 1.1 tensored with that reference, gives vector error at most $\epsilon$. For the identity branch, write a system-reference vector as $\sum_jx_j\otimes f_j$ in an orthonormal reference basis [F15]; [F11] makes its squared error the sum $\sum_j\|(I-U_H(t))x_j\|^2\le(\epsilon/3)^2\sum_j\|x_j\|^2$, justifying that extension explicitly. Then [F12] bounds the joint pure-state trace distance by $\epsilon$. The difference of the two joint density operators is Hermitian, so applying partial-trace contractivity [F13] over all work registers preserves this bound.

For a general input density operator, [F8]–[F9] give an orthonormal eigenbasis $(e_j)$ with nonnegative eigenvalues $\lambda_j$; [F14] and trace one imply $\sum_j\lambda_j=1$. Take an auxiliary reference space with orthonormal basis $(f_j)$, which exists by [F15], and set $\Psi=\sum_j\sqrt{\lambda_j}\,e_j\otimes f_j$. By the product inner product [F11], $\|\Psi\|^2=\sum_j\lambda_j=1$. In the product basis, its projector has entries $X_{(i,j),(i',j')}=\sqrt{\lambda_i\lambda_{i'}}\,\mathbf1_{i=j}\mathbf1_{i'=j'}$. The coordinate rule [F10] gives $(\operatorname{Tr}_{\rm ref}X)_{ii'}=\sum_jX_{(i,j),(i',j)}$, which is $\lambda_i$ if $i=i'$ and $0$ otherwise, exactly the matrix of $\rho$. Thus $\Psi$ purifies $\rho$. Apply step 4.1 with the original reference and this purifying reference, then trace out the work registers and the purifying register; [F13] again preserves the bound. Therefore the reduced outputs for $\rho$ differ in trace distance by at most $\epsilon$.

In each segment the chronological OAA circuit has two forward $W$ factors, one $W^\dagger$ factor, and two reflections [L1]. Expanding each $W=P^\dagger S_{\rm sel}P$ gives three PREPARE and three PREPARE$^\dagger$ calls, two SELECT and one SELECT$^\dagger$ call per segment. In the indexed term-query implementation [L1], a length-$k$ tuple acts by processing its labels in reverse order, so its $K$ conditionally active positions implement exactly $V_{j_1}\cdots V_{j_k}$. The phase and invalid-label rules are separately specified. Thus each SELECT or its adjoint uses at most $K$ controlled indexed term calls and the total is at most $3rK$. If only individual controlled $V_j$ are used to assemble a multiplexer, apply the $j$th unitary conditioned on label equality, for every $j<m$: exactly one block is active on each valid label, so this implements the same direct sum with at most $m$ individual calls per indexed call. This gives $3rmK$ individual calls with the declared label/routing/phase costs; no such decomposition bound is inferred for an arbitrary supplied SELECT. The expanded coefficient list has $N_K=\sum_{k=0}^Km^k$ ordered terms and two retained padding labels, giving the stated widths. Internal work and all other resource coordinates are charged as in [F7]. The identity branch has no queries or retained segment registers.

The register's alphabet is the ordered set $\{0,\ldots,d-1\}$.

For $n\ge0$, the $n$-qubit register is the ordered tensor product over

module tensor product ([[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]),
with its complex-module structure and finite iterated/empty-product conventions
from [[thm-commutative-ring-module-structure-on-a-tensor-product]] and
[[cor-finite-iterated-tensor-products-represent-multilinear-maps]]. The tuple of
bit positions is ordered lexicographically, with the first wire as the most
significant position; the product-basis theorem below establishes the
corresponding elementary tensors as a basis. For $n=0$, the empty tensor

All complex inner products in this track use the root convention: they are
linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second

space, define the Dirac pairing by

$$\langle x|y\rangle_D:=\langle y,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}.$$

The ket $|x\rangle$ denotes the vector $x$. The bra $\langle x|$ denotes the
linear functional $z\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle_{\mathrm{root}}$.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H,K$, vectors $y\in H$ and

$$|x\rangle\langle y|:H\to K,\qquad z\mapsto\langle z,y\rangle_{H,\mathrm{root}}x.$$

Given ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and $K$, its coordinate matrix is
$[x][y]^\dagger$, where $[x]$ and $[y]$ are the corresponding coordinate
columns and $M^\dagger:=\overline M^{\mathsf T}$ is the conjugate transpose.
The coordinate assertion is established in
[[thm-qc-dirac-notation-coordinate-identity]].

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and let $\psi\in H$ be a unit vector. Then $\Pi_\psi=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$ is a rank-one orthogonal projection, and $\Pi_{\lambda\psi}=\Pi_\psi$ for every $|\lambda|=1$. Therefore $R_\psi=2\Pi_\psi-I$ and $S_\psi=I-2\Pi_\psi$ are well-defined on the ray. Standalone they differ by the global scalar $-1$; when controlled in control-first order,

$$C(S_\psi)=(Z_C)C(R_\psi),\qquad Z_C=\operatorname{diag}(I,-I).$$

Let $C=Q_2$ be the control qubit with ordered basis $|0\rangle,|1\rangle$, and set $|\pm\rangle=(|0\rangle\pm|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$. Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and let $\Pi$ be an orthogonal projection on $H$. Fix the two signs

$$R_\Pi:=2\Pi-I,\qquad S_\Pi:=I-2\Pi=-R_\Pi.$$

Thus $R_\Pi$ acts as $+I$ on $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$ and $-I$ on $\ker\Pi$; $S_\Pi$ reverses those signs. They are not interchangeable inside a controlled block. For a unit vector $\psi$, the rank-one reflection is $R_\psi=2|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|-I$ with the Dirac convention of [[def-qc-dirac-notation-conversion]].

An access model counts a direct reflection as one primitive call only when that call is explicitly declared. Controlled reflection access is a separate declaration. If $|0\rangle$ is a specified unit input in the same space $H$, the state is prepared as $\psi=U|0\rangle$ for a declared unitary $U$, and a reflection is implemented by conjugating $R_0=2|0\rangle\langle0|-I$, the construction is $UR_0U^\dagger$ and its cost must include the calls to $U$, $R_0$, and $U^\dagger$. A state vector or matrix description alone implies neither an efficient reflection nor inverse access.

Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex-inner-product space and let $\Pi$ be an orthogonal projection. The operators $R_\Pi=2\Pi-I$ and $S_\Pi=I-2\Pi$ are self-adjoint unitary involutions, with $R_\Pi=-S_\Pi$. On $\operatorname{ran}\Pi$ they act as $+I$ and $-I$, respectively; on $\ker\Pi$ they act as $-I$ and $+I$. In control-first order,

$$C(S_\Pi)=(Z_C)C(R_\Pi),\qquad Z_C:=\operatorname{diag}(I_H,-I_H)=Z\otimes I_H.$$

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

Let $V:H\to K$ be a linear isometry between finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces whose pairings are linear in the first argument. Then $\langle Vx,Vy\rangle_K=\langle x,y\rangle_H$ for all $x,y\in H$.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$ 

For the empty tensor, the right side is the empty product $1$, giving the
standard inner product on $\mathbb C$.

For a permutation $\sigma$ of the $n$ factor positions, the **wire permutation**
$P_\sigma$ maps the product basis vector indexed by
$(i_0,\ldots,i_{n-1})$ to the product basis vector whose output factor order is
$(\sigma(0),\ldots,\sigma(n-1))$. It is extended linearly; for $n=0$ it is the
identity on $\mathbb C$. The extension is a linear map in the sense of
[[def-linear-map]].
